title: 儒家思想入门：仁、义、礼、智的核心智慧 | What Is Confucianism: A Complete Introduction
titleEn: What Is Confucianism: A Complete Introduction to China's Most Influential Philosophy
author: knowphilosophers.site

sections.heading: The Philosophy That Shaped East Asian Civilization
sections.body:
Confucianism is not just a philosophy — it is the ethical, social, and political backbone of East Asian civilization for over two millennia. Founded by Confucius (Kongzi, 孔子, 551-479 BC) in ancient China, it has profoundly shaped the cultures of China, Korea, Japan, and Vietnam — influencing everything from family structures and educational systems to government, business, and daily etiquette.

Unlike Western philosophies that often begin with abstract metaphysical questions, Confucianism begins with a deeply practical concern: how can human beings live together in harmony? Its answer is a vision of ethical cultivation — through learning, ritual, and relationships — that transforms individuals into exemplary persons (junzi, 君子) whose virtue radiates outward to order families, communities, and entire states.

This guide introduces the core concepts of Confucianism: ren (benevolence), yi (righteousness), li (ritual propriety), zhi (wisdom), and the Five Relationships. Whether you're encountering Confucianism for the first time or deepening your understanding, you'll find here both the ancient wisdom and the contemporary relevance of one of the world's great philosophical traditions.
sections.bodyEn: Confucianism is the ethical backbone of East Asian civilization. Founded by Confucius (551-479 BC), it offers a vision of ethical cultivation through learning, ritual, and relationships — transforming individuals into exemplary persons whose virtue radiates outward to harmonize the world.

sections.heading: 1. Ren (仁): Benevolence, Humaneness, Human-heartedness
sections.body:
Ren is the central concept of Confucian ethics. The Chinese character is composed of 'person' (人) and 'two' (二), suggesting that ren is fundamentally relational — it is the quality of being fully human in relation to others.

Confucius defines ren in various ways throughout the Analects (Lunyu):

- 'Ren is to love others' (Analects 12.22)
- 'To overcome the self and return to ritual propriety is ren' (Analects 12.1)
- 'Do not impose on others what you yourself do not desire' (Analects 15.24) — the negative formulation of the Golden Rule, predating its positive formulation in Christianity
- 'The person of ren, wishing to establish themselves, establishes others; wishing to succeed, helps others succeed' (Analects 6.30)

Ren is not a momentary feeling of kindness but a cultivated disposition — a deep, steady orientation toward the well-being of others. It is expressed not primarily in words or emotions but in conduct. The person of ren treats every human interaction — from the most intimate family relationship to the most distant political encounter — as an opportunity to manifest their humanity.

Confucius was careful to note that ren is both rare and accessible. 'Is ren far away? When I desire ren, ren arrives' (Analects 7.30). The capacity for ren is innate; its cultivation is a lifelong project.
sections.bodyEn: Ren (仁) is the core Confucian virtue — benevolent, relational, human-hearted. Defined in the Analects as 'to love others,' it is not a fleeting feeling but a cultivated disposition expressed in conduct. 'Do not impose on others what you yourself do not desire.' The capacity is innate; the cultivation is lifelong.

sections.heading: 2. Li (礼): Ritual, Propriety, and the Shape of Civilization
sections.body:
If ren is the inner spirit of Confucianism, li (礼) is its outer form. Li encompasses ritual, ceremony, etiquette, and social norms — the entire framework of civilized behavior through which ren is expressed and cultivated.

To modern Western readers, 'ritual' can sound hollow or oppressive — empty formality. But for Confucius, li is the essential vehicle of moral development. By performing the rites with sincerity and attention — bowing respectfully, observing mourning customs, using proper forms of address — one gradually internalizes the attitudes that the rites embody: reverence, care, humility.

Confucius says: 'If you are respectful but lack li, you will be wearisome. If you are cautious but lack li, you will be timid. If you are courageous but lack li, you will be unruly' (Analects 8.2). Li is not the enemy of genuine feeling — it is what gives raw feeling its proper expression, just as a musical instrument gives form to sound.

This is why Confucius emphasizes the aesthetic dimension of li. Properly performed ritual is beautiful — it creates harmony, like a well-conducted orchestra. The ideal society, for Confucius, is one in which li permeates every relationship, and every interaction becomes a small performance of shared humanity.
sections.bodyEn: Li (礼) — ritual propriety — is the outer form through which ren is expressed and cultivated. Far from hollow formality, li gives raw feeling its proper expression. 'Respect without li is wearisome; courage without li is unruly.' Properly performed, li creates harmony like a well-conducted orchestra.

sections.heading: 3. The Five Relationships and Filial Piety
sections.body:
Confucian ethics is structured around the Five Relationships (wulun, 五伦), which map the basic forms of human social life:

1. **Ruler and Subject** — governed by loyalty and righteousness (yi, 义)
2. **Parent and Child** — governed by affection and filial piety (xiao, 孝)
3. **Husband and Wife** — governed by differentiation of roles and mutual respect
4. **Elder and Younger Sibling** — governed by precedence and deference (ti, 悌)
5. **Friend and Friend** — governed by trust and faithfulness (xin, 信)

Filial piety (xiao) deserves special attention. For Confucius, the family is the root of all virtue — the primary school of ethical life. 'A youth, when at home, should be filial; when abroad, respectful to elders. He should be earnest and truthful. He should overflow in love to all and cultivate the friendship of the good' (Analects 1.6).

The logic is developmental: you first learn to love and respect within the family, then extend these capacities outward. A person who does not honor their parents cannot genuinely respect their ruler or care for their community. The family is not a retreat from public life; it is the training ground for public life.

Critics have noted that the Five Relationships encode hierarchical assumptions. But Confucius himself emphasized reciprocity: the ruler must be worthy of the subject's loyalty; the parent must be worthy of the child's devotion. 'Let the ruler be a ruler, the minister a minister, the father a father, the son a son' (Analects 12.11) — each role carries both rights and responsibilities.
sections.bodyEn: The Five Relationships structure Confucian social ethics. Filial piety (xiao) is the root: the family is the primary school of ethical life. But roles carry reciprocal responsibilities — the ruler must be worthy of loyalty, the parent of devotion. It is a vision of mutual obligation, not one-way authority.

sections.heading: 4. The Junzi: The Exemplary Person
sections.body:
The ideal human being in Confucianism is the junzi (君子), often translated as 'gentleman,' 'exemplary person,' or 'noble person.' The junzi is not born — they are made, through a lifetime of learning, self-cultivation, and moral practice.

Confucius contrasts the junzi with the 'small person' (xiaoren, 小人) not in terms of social class but of moral orientation: 'The junzi understands what is right; the small person understands what is profitable' (Analects 4.16). 'The junzi is calm and at ease; the small person is always anxious and full of worry' (Analects 7.37). 'The junzi seeks it in themselves; the small person seeks it in others' (Analects 15.21).

The junzi embodies what Confucius describes as 'learning for the sake of the self' — education that transforms character, not education that merely accumulates information or credentials. This is perhaps the most radical dimension of Confucianism: the conviction that anyone, regardless of birth, can become a junzi through dedicated effort.

Confucius himself was the model: 'At fifteen I set my heart on learning; at thirty I took my stand; at forty I had no doubts; at fifty I knew the decree of Heaven; at sixty my ear was obedient; at seventy I could follow my heart's desires without overstepping the line' (Analects 2.4). The path is long but open to all.
sections.bodyEn: The junzi (exemplary person) is the Confucian ideal — made through learning and self-cultivation, not through birth. 'The junzi understands what is right; the small person understands what is profitable.' Anyone, regardless of birth, can become a junzi through dedicated effort.
